sources.citation: Drinfeld, Andrey. 2024. A grammar of Aro, a Torricelli language of Papua New Guinea. PhD dissertation, University at Buffalo, SUNY. 671 pp.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: NOT an Aruek source: it describes Aro (Aroic, Core Kombioic; no ISO code, subsumed under 'tei'/torr1259). Aruek is mentioned only pp. 8-9 (Dryer in prep. classification: Core Kombioic = Aroic {Aro, Mukweym, Orok} + Eitiep + Aruek + Kombio) and pp. 25-26 ('according to my consultants, the Aro speaking area does not share a boundary with the Aruek speaking area (it seems that the Aruek language is, in fact, spoken significantly further to the east)'). No Aruek data. For Aro itself, sec. 2.5 pp. 117-128: stress is predictable from syllable weight (four weights), rightmost weight-1 syllable extra…

sources.note: Nothing on stress. Aruek appears only in the classification table (p. 773, Kombio Family, 614 speakers). The general phonological characterisation of Torricelli languages (p. 769: three places of articulation, usually no voicing contrast, 5-8 vowels, many fricatives) does not mention stress; p. 774: 'None of the languages of the Torricelli Phylum have yet been studied in great detail.'

sources.note: Wordlist only: ~75 items in ASJPcode (e.g. 1 I ak, 2 you yik, 21 dog 5imbwa, 75 water w3mbEp, 82 fire sutE). ASJPcode does not encode stress or tone, and the entry has no prose; no statement and no stress marks. It does show that Laycock's notebook list is substantial (75+ items), so if Laycock marked stress in the original (PARADISEC DL2-013, login-gated) that would be the only place it survives.
